entities.summary:
The Gothic War of 376–382 was a pivotal conflict in the ancient world, a brutal and devastating series of battles between the Goths and the Eastern Roman Empire, fought on the blood-soaked plains of Thrace during the late 4th century. This war marked a turning point in Roman history, as the empire's military power began to wane, and its grip on the Balkans weakened, paving the way for the subsequent Huns' invasion. The war was ignited by the Huns' pressure on the Goths, who had been displaced from their homeland in modern-day Russia and Ukraine. As the Goths, led by Alatheus and Saphrax, poured into the Roman Empire, they were met with fierce resistance from the Roman legions, led by the Emperor Valens. The war raged on for six years, from 376 to 382, with both sides suffering heavy losses. The Gothic War of 376–382 ended with the Goths being granted safe passage into the empire, but at a steep price: they were allowed to settle within Roman borders, only to eventually turn against their new hosts, sparking a series of bloody conflicts that would shake the Roman Empire to its foundations. 

 The war had far-reaching consequences, as it led to the weakening of the Eastern Roman Empire and the eventual rise of the Huns, who would go on to conquer much of Europe. The war also marked a significant shift in the balance of power in the ancient world, as the Goths and the Huns began to play a more prominent role in shaping the fate of the Roman Empire. 

 The Gothic War of 376–382 left an indelible mark on world history, as it marked the beginning of the end of the Roman Empire's dominance and paved the way for the emergence of new powers in the ancient world. 

 The war's legacy can be seen in the numerous cultural and historical artifacts that have survived to this day, including the writings of the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus, who chronicled the war in his magnum opus, 'The Res Gestae'.
